blocks.text: Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma

inline.s: The “in accord with the Dharma” of “upholding the Dharma” means: “All marks whatsoever are delusive and false. If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata.”

[At that time Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! What should this sutra be named? How should we uphold and practice it? The Buddha told Subhuti: This sutra is named the Diamond Prajna Paramita. By this name you should uphold it.]

At this time Subhuti asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! How should this sutra be named? How should we uphold and practice it? The Buddha told Subhuti: This sutra is named the Diamond Prajna Paramita. You should uphold and practice it by this name—the Diamond Prajna Paramita (reaching the shore of nirvana by the wondrous wisdom of the diamond). For this is the mind-dharma that enables you to leave illusion and become a Buddha by the wondrous wisdom of the diamond.

The core of practice is leaving illusion, and so below the World-Honored One enumerates that prajna paramita is illusion, that the Tathagata’s teaching of the Dharma is illusion, that dust-motes are illusion, that the world is illusion, and that the thirty-two marks are illusion as well. This chapter closes with the boundless merit and virtue of upholding this sutra, showing that illusions are not entirely nonexistent: in essence they have no substance, yet in appearance they exist. This is lest those who misunderstand fall into the abyss of annihilationism.

Again and again in this sutra the World-Honored One teaches: all is illusion, and we should cling neither to existence (clinging to marks) nor to nonexistence (annihilating marks), but should cultivate the real by means of the provisional and leave illusion by means of illusion. Yet living beings, through beginningless kalpas and life after life, either cling to existence or cling to nonexistence; their habitual defilement is too heavy. Though now they understand in principle, the moment circumstances arise they are deluded again. Therefore the World-Honored One wants us to use diamond-like wisdom to contemplate and examine ourselves and to contemplate and examine circumstances, closely and unremittingly, turning delusion into awakening, reaching the shore of nirvana and waking from the dream of ignorance. The Sixth Patriarch said: “In the dark house of affliction, one must always give rise to the sun of wisdom.” This sun of wisdom is the diamond prajna.
[Why is this? Subhuti! What the Buddha speaks of as prajna paramita is not prajna paramita; therefore it is called prajna paramita.]

The World-Honored One continued: What is the reason for this? Because “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false,” even prajna paramita itself is an illusion (breaking the mark of dharmas). In this dream of ignorance there is not one thing that is not an illusion, and so one must quickly escape by means of the diamond prajna paramita.

Lest living beings fail to understand and take prajna paramita as real, cultivating with clinging to marks and thinking that there is a prajna paramita to cultivate and a nirvana to attain, the World-Honored One admonishes: Subhuti! The prajna paramita spoken of by the Buddha is also an illusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and all living beings of the final age should keep far from every illusory and false realm. Because of firmly and persistently maintaining the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like an illusion must likewise be kept far from; the keeping far away that is an illusion must likewise be kept far from; the keeping far from the illusion of keeping far away must likewise be kept far from; when one reaches having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.” This means: toward every illusory and false realm one should firmly and persistently maintain the mind of keeping far away, but since the mind is an illusion, the mind of keeping far away must also be kept far from; the keeping far away from the “mind of keeping far away” is likewise an illusion, so this keeping far away must also be kept far from; and this keeping far away is likewise an illusion, so from this keeping far away one must again keep far. Only when one reaches having nothing to keep far from are all illusions removed. Therefore leaving illusion must be done layer by layer, until one reaches having nothing to keep far from, and only then can all illusions be extinguished. Hence the ancients said: “Set up and at once break down; fall into neither extreme.”

The prajna paramita spoken of by the Buddha is to leave marks and realize nirvana by prajna wisdom, and so accomplish the Buddha Way. But if one again takes prajna paramita as real and cultivates with clinging to marks (conditioned dharmas), then one can never reach the shore of nirvana. The principles that the preceding sutra text sets forth again and again are here taken one layer deeper. This is what is meant by: “Simply exhaust (do away with) ordinary sentiment; there is no other sagely understanding.” From this one may also feel the Buddha’s loving kindness and painstaking care for living beings. Therefore the venerable Subhuti praised him, saying: “The Tathagata excellently cares for all bodhisattvas and excellently entrusts all bodhisattvas.”
The Great Prajna Paramita Sutra

fascicle 548, says: “The gods should know that the dharma I have realized is precisely prajna paramita. This dharma is most profound: it is neither that which realizes nor that which is realized; there is no place of realization and no time of realization.” The Great Prajna Paramita Sutra

fascicle 416, says: “How should a bodhisattva-mahasattva keep far from all clinging to dharmas? Shanxian (that is, Subhuti), because a bodhisattva-mahasattva contemplates the nature of all dharmas as like empty space and unattainable, therefore a bodhisattva-mahasattva should keep far from all clinging to dharmas.” The Great Prajna Paramita Sutra
fascicle 1

the Chapter on Learning and Contemplation, says: “All bodhisattva-mahasattvas should take non-clinging as their skillful means and perfect prajna paramita, because the nature and marks of all dharmas are unattainable.”
[Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has spoken nothing.]
The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata spoken the Dharma? Subhuti replied: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has not spoken the Dharma.

The Buddha taught the sutras and spoke the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet he says he has not spoken the Dharma. This has several layers of profound meaning: 1. The Tathagata’s teaching of the Dharma is a matter within the dream of ignorance and is not truly existent; 2. The Tathagata’s teaching of the Dharma is a finger pointing at the moon, not the Dharma itself; one must not be mired in the words but should take up the meaning beyond the words; 3. All Buddhas of the ten directions and three times teach in this way—Buddha after Buddha the Way is the same, dharma after dharma it is thus; this is not the World-Honored One’s own invention; 4. The World-Honored One has no contriving mind: he speaks yet does not speak.

Even so, the Tathagata’s teaching of the Dharma can guide living beings out of illusion: “Therefore one should not grasp dharmas, nor should one grasp non-dharmas.” The World-Honored One’s teaching is a road, and those who cultivate the Way must walk along it before they have any real benefit.

Prajna paramita is an illusion, and the Tathagata’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise an illusion. Though both are illusions, we must use them to leave illusion, using them without clinging. Here the World-Honored One again clarifies leaving illusion by means of illusion.

[Subhuti! What do you think—are all the dust-motes in a trichiliocosm many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Subhuti! All the dust-motes the Tathagata speaks of are not dust-motes; therefore they are called dust-motes. The world the Tathagata speaks of is not the world; therefore it is called the world.]

The Buddha asked: Subhuti! What do you think—are all the dust-motes of a trichiliocosm many? Subhuti replied: Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: Subhuti! All the dust-motes (with marks) the Tathagata speaks of as not dust-motes (without substance); therefore they are called dust-motes (they are illusion). The world the Tathagata speaks of (with marks) is not the world (without substance); therefore it is called the world (it is illusion).
This says that dust-motes (the small) are illusion, and the world (the great) is also illusion.

[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by way of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by way of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? What the Tathagata speaks of as the thirty-two marks is no marks; therefore it is called the thirty-two marks.]

The Buddha asked: Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by way of the thirty-two marks? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by way of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The thirty-two marks the Tathagata speaks of (with marks) are not the thirty-two marks (without substance); therefore they are called the thirty-two marks (they are illusion).
This says that although the thirty-two marks are the most excellent and beautiful bodily marks, they are also illusion. In the Maha Prajna Paramita Sutra

fascicle 25, the Buddha says: “When a bodhisattva-mahasattva is mindful of the Buddha, he is not mindful by way of the thirty-two marks, nor is he mindful of the golden-colored body, nor of the ten-foot light, nor of the eighty subsidiary marks. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s body is without intrinsic nature.”

[The thirty-two marks] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great person. The inner virtues of a Buddha or of a wheel-turning sage king are manifested in the bodily marks in thirty-two ways, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, and not one of them is other than excellent and beautiful.

[Subhuti! If a good man or good woman gives in giving bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and if again there is a person who, in this sutra, upholds even a four-line verse and explains it to others, that person’s merit is very great.]

The Buddha said: Subhuti! If a good man or good woman gives in giving bodies and lives as many times over as the sands of the Ganges, the merit and virtue of that giving is far less than that of one who, in this sutra, upholds even a single verse (four lines of sutra text) and explains it to others.
[Giving bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges] Giving away life as many times over as the sands of the Ganges (there is only one life in a lifetime).

In the dream of ignorance all dharmas are illusion. Prajna paramita is an illusion, the Dharma spoken by the Tathagata is an illusion, and even dust-motes, the world and the Buddha’s thirty-two marks are all illusions as well. Therefore one who upholds this sutra and understands the unconditioned dharma, leaving marks and dwelling nowhere, has boundless merit and virtue.

Freedom from affliction is called “stillness”; freedom from birth and death is called “extinction.” The state in which there is neither affliction nor birth and death is nirvana. “Leaving marks and quiescent extinction” is what the following sutra text says: “Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha.”

[At that time Subhuti, having heard this sutra spoken, deeply understood its meaning and purport, and weeping and lamenting with tears, said to the Buddha: How rare, World-Honored One! The Buddha has spoken such a profound sutra. From of old, though I have attained the wisdom eye, I have never heard such a sutra.]

At this time Subhuti, having heard the wondrous principle spoken by the World-Honored One and deeply understood the meaning and purport of this sutra, with grief and joy intermingled and weeping tears of gratitude, praised the Buddha: ‘How unsurpassed, World-Honored One! You have spoken a sutra so profound, subtle and penetrating. From of old, though I have attained the wisdom eye, I have never heard such a sutra!’

[Profound sutra] This says that the theory, method and realm of this sutra are extremely profound, subtle and penetrating. [Wisdom eye] The eye of wisdom, realized by the two vehicles; the wisdom that knows the equal nature of all dharmas as empty. [Nature is empty] All things and dharmas are originally empty in nature, with no substantial entity to be attained.

What caused Subhuti thus to mingle grief and joy and weep tears of gratitude? His joy was that today he had heard the most complete, most direct and most real dharma of becoming a Buddha, and so the elder, deeply understanding its meaning and purport, says below: “Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha.” His grief was that through beginningless kalpas he had had no way to hear the great Dharma, and so had sunk into delusion until now. The elder rejoices without end!
Chen dynasty

Paramartha’s translation: “At that time Subhuti, whose life was pure, because the dharma-benefit was swift, at once wept in sorrow.” The Diamond Sutra is a swift dharma; this is the practice of the One Buddha Vehicle: seeing the nature (“If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata”), eliminating habit (“One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), and leaving all marks to straightaway realize Buddhahood (“Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha”).
[Swift dharma] A rapid and perfect dharma.

The theory, realm and method spoken of in this sutra are not only suited to beginners (“After the Tathagata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit,” and they will be able to believe, understand, receive and practice it), but also run straight through to the Buddha fruit: awakening to the unconditioned dharma, without passing through the stages (without passing through the fifty-two stages), straightaway realizing Buddhahood. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records: “The Master (Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch) constantly urged monks and laypeople: simply uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and straightaway realize Buddhahood.” It is precisely this:

The unsurpassed, profound and wondrous Dharma,
Hard to encounter through hundreds of thousands of kalpas,

[World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, they at once give rise to the true mark. You should know that such people accomplish the foremost and rarest merit and virtue. World-Honored One! This true mark is no mark; therefore the Tathagata calls it the true mark.]

World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, they at once give rise to the true mark. You should know that such people accomplish the foremost and rarest merit and virtue.”

—Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! If there are yet other people who hear this sutra with pure faith, they at once awaken to the true mark (the actual state in which all things in the universe are entirely illusion). You should know that such a person accomplishes the most excellent merit and virtue.

[If again there are people] If there are still other people. This follows directly on the preceding: I, Subhuti, having heard this sutra spoken, deeply understood its meaning and purport and benefited beyond compare; if there are yet other people who hear this sutra, .... [Faith] The mind that gives rise to belief in the dharma heard, deeply believing without doubt. [Purity of faith] Hearing this sutra and deeply believing without doubt, one then sees illusion and at once leaves it, closely examining and testing it amid circumstances (not giving rise to a mind dwelling in forms, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas, giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere); the clouds of delusion disperse, the light of the nature appears, and the mind attains purity. [True mark] The true mark is the actual state that “all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing to be found.” The Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says: “What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing to be found.” [At once give rise to the true mark] That is, one awakens to the actual state in which all things in the universe are entirely illusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Within the true mark there is in truth no bodhisattva and no living being. Why is this? Bodhisattvas and living beings are all illusory transformations.” In the Great Parinirvana Sutra
fascicle 40

the Chapter on Kaundinya, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, that is called the true mark, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the supreme meaning, that is called supreme emptiness.” [Foremost and rarest] Most excellent; here “rare” means excellent.

The whole art of Buddhadharma lies in awakening—giving rise to the true mark. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra the Buddha says: “The true mark of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still, is precisely the Buddha Way.” The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary person; when the following thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to circumstances, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves circumstances, that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are delusive and false. If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata.”
World-Honored One! This true mark is no mark; therefore the Tathagata calls it the true mark.”
—Next, Subhuti said: World-Honored One! This true mark is without marks (the true mark is without marks), and so the Tathagata says it is the true mark.
This is supreme emptiness—the emptiness of the middle-way true mark that is neither empty nor existent, in which even the true mark is not clung to.
In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

the Chapter on the True Mark of All Dharmas, the First, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, without marks and without contrivance.” This is to look at all dharmas in terms of their substance. To one in the dream of ignorance, all dharmas have marks; but to one with wakened eyes, there is nothing at all. The Direct Explanation of the True Mind says: “It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky. Or a person without disease says: there are no sky-flowers. The sick one does not believe it. If the eye disease is gone, the sky-flowers vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe there are no flowers.” Living beings, within serene non-arising, see only birth and death (marks); the Buddhas, within manifest birth and death, see only non-arising (no marks).
[The true mark is without marks] The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

fascicle 14, says: “If one leaves home and observes the precepts, does not manage worldly affairs, and constantly contemplates all dharmas as to their true mark being without marks; though at first of dull faculties, one gradually becomes sharp. Through various causes and conditions such as these, it is called observing the precepts giving rise to prajna paramita. Such things are called shila paramita giving rise to the six paramitas.”
[Shila paramita] The paramita of observing the precepts.

[World-Honored One! I now hear such a sutra, and to believe, understand, receive and uphold it is not difficult. But in a future age, in the last five hundred years, if there are living beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive and uphold it, such people are foremost and rare.]

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! Now that I hear such a profound sutra, to believe, understand, receive and uphold it is not difficult. But if in the fifth five hundred years after the Tathagata’s extinction and thereafter, there are living beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive and uphold it, such people are foremost and most excellent.

[In a future age, in the last five hundred years] This means the same as “after the Tathagata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years” in Chapter Six: the fifth five hundred years after the Tathagata’s extinction and thereafter. [If there are living beings] If there are living beings. “If” is a conjunction, equivalent to “if” or “supposing.”

[Why is this? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life are no marks. Why is this? Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha.]
This passage of sutra text clarifies: why “such a person is foremost and rare.”

Why is this? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life are no marks.”

—Why is such a person foremost and most excellent? Because he no longer has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life. Why is there no mark of a self, mark of a person, mark of a living being or mark of a life? Because the mark of a self (with marks) is not the mark of a self (without substance), and the mark of a self is illusion; the mark of a person, mark of a living being and mark of a life (with marks) are not the mark of a person, mark of a living being and mark of a life (without substance), and the mark of a person, mark of a living being and mark of a life are illusion.

This means: because such a person believes, understands, receives and upholds this sutra, and has put “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false” into practice in his own thoughts, words and deeds, he should no longer have these four illusory marks.
Why is this? Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha.”
—Why is it said that such a person is foremost and most excellent? Because, having left all marks,
he is at once named a Buddha.
[Is at once named a Buddha] That is, he is at once named a Buddha. Here the word “zhu” (all) functions like “zhi” (him), as in the example: “Neng shi zhu hu?” (Can you serve him?)

From this we may know: how does one become a Buddha? Leaving all marks—this is the way to become a Buddha. What is called leaving marks is seeing marks without being deluded and not being turned about by circumstances; not being turned about by any circumstance is to be a Buddha. Chapter Seven says: “All sages and saints are distinguished by the unconditioned dharma.” That is to say: all sages and saints are distinguished according to the degree to which they are not turned about by circumstances (leaving marks).

[Leaving marks] Realizing that marks are all illusory, and so being without love and hate, taking and rejecting. [Clinging to marks] Taking marks as real, and so having love and hate, taking and rejecting.

Leaving all marks” has two great contents: 1. Breaking the clinging to a self and cutting off ordinary sentiment; 2. Breaking the clinging to dharmas and removing sagely understanding. In the Lotus Sutra

the Chapter on Skillful Means, the Second, the Buddha says: “Shariputra! Since I became a Buddha, with various causes and conditions and various parables I have widely expounded teachings, with countless skillful means guiding living beings and causing them to leave all clingings.” Leaving all clingings is leaving all marks.

The venerable Subhuti, deeply understanding the meaning and purport, awakened to the foremost and rarest dharma: leaving marks (seeing marks without being deluded and not being turned about by circumstances). Leaving marks—this is the unconditioned dharma. This method of practice differs from the methods of the three vehicles that he knew (the shravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle and the bodhisattva vehicle); this is the mind-dharma of the One Buddha Vehicle, the most direct and most perfect and sudden dharma, which realizes Buddhahood straightaway without passing through the fifty-two stages.

The practice method of this sutra is the illusion-like samadhi spoken of by the Buddha in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment: “Knowing illusion, one at once leaves it, without using skillful means; leaving illusion, one is at once awakened, and there are no gradual stages either.”

One thing especially to note: in the course of leaving illusion, one must by all means leave illusion by means of illusion, and must never, intending to leave, instead enter. For example, giving without dwelling in marks is leaving illusion by means of illusion, whereas giving while dwelling in marks is entering illusion by means of illusion, seeking to rise and instead falling.

The crux of leaving illusion is leaving desire, which should be done first of all. Our Buddha taught people to transcend the world and took the practice of leaving desire as the foremost. Hence it is said: “Leaving desire and attaining stillness is the foremost of all.” (The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha)

Leaving marks (seeing marks without being deluded and not being turned about by circumstances) is the entire purport of this sutra. The core of practicing the Diamond Sutra is leaving marks—knowing illusion, one at once leaves it; leaving again and again, one reaches having nothing to leave, and all illusions are removed; once all illusions are removed and the dream of ignorance ends, one is called a Buddha. In this sutra the World-Honored One also warns us again and again: in the course of leaving illusion, one must by all means use illusion to extinguish illusion, and never use illusion to enter illusion.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and all living beings of the final age should keep far from every illusory and false realm. Because of firmly maintaining the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like an illusion must likewise be kept far from; the keeping far away that is an illusion must likewise be kept far from; the keeping far from the illusion of keeping far away must likewise be kept far from; when one reaches having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.”
Question: How does one leave all marks?

Answer: “Leaving all marks is called being a Buddha.” The corresponding translation by the Tripitaka Master Paramartha, the Diamond Prajna Paramita Sutra, reads: “The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are liberated from all notions without remainder.” Therefore leaving marks is leaving notions. As soon as a notion arises, one should at once see through it and let it go. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing illusion, one at once leaves it, without using skillful means; leaving illusion, one is at once awakened, and there are no gradual stages either.” The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: “The Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is entirely without notion and without thought.”
[The Buddha told Subhuti: It is so! It is so! If again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such people are most rare.]
The Buddha told Subhuti: It is so! It is so!”
—The Buddha said to Subhuti: It is so! It is so!
It is so! It is so!”—this is the World-Honored One greatly praising Subhuti’s experience and understanding as set forth above.
If again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such people are most rare.”
—If there are yet other people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such people are most rare.

[If again there are people] This is the World-Honored One continuing from Subhuti’s speaking of his own believing, understanding, receiving and upholding, and of someone in the last five hundred years believing, understanding, receiving and upholding (to be able to believe, understand, receive and uphold, one certainly hears this sutra without being startled, terrified or afraid), saying: if there are yet other people .....

Why is it said that those who “hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid” are most rare? Because this sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are delusive and false.” All Buddha worlds have marks, and so all Buddha worlds are illusions. This is more astonishing by I know not how many times than Copernicus’s heliocentric theory in those days! Therefore those who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid are truly most rare.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth and death and nirvana, ordinary people and all Buddhas, are alike the mark of a flower in the sky.” “All Buddha worlds are like flowers in empty space.” It also says: “Within it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asankhyeyas, inexpressible, Ganges-sands of Buddha worlds are like flowers in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion.” The Maha Prajna Paramita Sutra

the Chapter on Practicing in Conformity, the Third, the Buddha says: “Therefore in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formation or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind; no form, sound, fragrance, taste, tangible objects or dharmas; no eye-realm up to no mind-consciousness realm; also no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, accumulation, extinction or path; also no wisdom and no attainment; no srotaapanna and no fruit of srotaapanna; no sakridagamin and no fruit of sakridagamin; no anagamin and no fruit of anagamin; no arhat and no fruit of arhat; no pratyekabuddha and no pratyekabuddha path; no Buddha and no Buddha path.”

Below, the World-Honored One continues to clarify: why is it that “if again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such people are most rare”?
[Why is this? Subhuti! What the Tathagata speaks of as the first paramita is not the first paramita; therefore it is called the first paramita.]

Why should you know that such people are most rare? Subhuti! The diamond prajna paramita (the first paramita) is also an illusion—the first paramita the Tathagata speaks of (with marks) is not the first paramita (without substance); therefore it is called the first paramita (it is illusion).
[The first paramita] That is, the dharma spoken of in this sutra—the diamond prajna paramita, also called the maha paramita. The Maha Prajna Paramita Sutra

fascicle 2, says: “The maha paramita is the bodhisattva-mahasattva’s prajna paramita, the venerable paramita, the first paramita, the victorious paramita, the wondrous paramita, the unsurpassed paramita, the unequaled paramita, the unequaled-among-unequaled paramita, the space-like paramita.” [Maha] In Chinese translation: great.

In the preceding chapter the World-Honored One already said that prajna paramita is an illusion (“What the Buddha speaks of as prajna paramita is not prajna paramita; therefore it is called prajna paramita”). Not only that, but even the dharma spoken of in this sutra—the diamond prajna paramita—is also an illusion.

Next the World-Honored One takes the paramita of patience as an example to show that the six perfections are also illusions, and that one should not cling to marks but should leave all marks; only then can the mind be without hindrance and cross beyond all suffering and distress.
[Subhuti! The paramita of patience, the Tathagata speaks of as not the paramita of patience; therefore it is called the paramita of patience.]

The World-Honored One also said: Subhuti! The paramita of patience (with marks), the Tathagata speaks of as not the paramita of patience (without substance); therefore it is called the paramita of patience (it is illusion). This says that the paramita of patience is an illusion, and one must not cling to the mark of the paramita of patience.

[The paramita of patience] That is, the perfection of patience among the six perfections (giving, observing the precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and prajna). The old translation of the six perfections is the six paramitas. “Paramita” means reaching the other shore; in Chinese it is translated “du” (the same as “crossing over”), meaning to cross over to the other shore (the shore of nirvana). “Ru” (insult, patience) ordinarily means suffering shame and suffering insult. In fact, in classical Chinese “ru” has another meaning: suffering setback and suffering harm. Master Xuanzang’s translation of the six perfections is: giving, pure precepts, patient endurance, diligence, quiet contemplation and prajna. This shows that “renru” (patience) means patient endurance. Therefore the paramita of patience is not giving rise to anger or hatred when people, things and circumstances go against one’s will (afflict and harm one). The mind of patience can guard against the invasion of outer circumstances, and so it is likened to clothing. A practitioner who puts on the robe of patience is like a warrior who has armor to protect his body and suffers no harm.

Therefore the key to dealing with affliction and harm is not to be turned about by circumstances but to turn the circumstances—knowing that affliction and harm are themselves illusion, not giving rise to hatred, aversion or rejection. Then the mind is without hindrance, crosses beyond all suffering and distress, and turns affliction into bodhi, receiving only the benefit and not the harm. Remember: the mara arises from the mind and is also extinguished by the mind. When insulted:

Think of it as exhausting karma. This karmic retribution is one’s own doing and one’s own receiving; one should not blame others. Moreover, once repaid it is finished, and the karmic debt of enmity is thereby wiped out at one stroke—a very good thing.

Think of it as a blessing. Realize that this is a blessing coming in reverse, coming to accomplish my practice of the Way. Mencius said: “When Heaven is about to confer a great responsibility on a man, it will first test his resolve, fatigue his muscles and bones, starve his body, empty his purse, and frustrate his undertakings, so as to move his mind and strengthen his nature, and increase what he is capable of.” For one who cultivates the Way, all people are accomplishing me; all are my benefactors, some through favorable conditions, some through adverse conditions. They are all bringing my practice of the Way to fulfillment; there is not even time to be grateful—how could one bear resentment? I have only benefactors, no enemies.

Take it as an examination question on the bodhi path. It both tests whether one’s practice is effective and, through this tempering, raises one’s practice to a higher floor; liberation then becomes more certain. Practitioners face such an examination question at every time and place: “All marks whatsoever are delusive and false.” “Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”—In the illusory realm, did you take it as real? Did your mind move? How your practice stands can be tested for yourself.

There are three levels to the practice of patience: 1. First endure, then transform; 2. Endure and transform at once; 3. Be wholly unaware. Here is an actual example of the practice of patience, “White Eyes Turned On Him, as if Bathed in the Spring Breeze”:
Elder Master Guangqin entered the back mountain at the age of

to practice austerities, without food or clothing, through thirteen winters and summers. Not long after he returned to Chengtian Chan Temple, the incense-offering money placed in the main hall was lost. When the supervising monk and the incense-lamp monk spread the news, the whole temple was in an uproar. Before he returned to the temple, the incense money had never been lost; not long after he came back, the incense money on which the whole temple depended for its livelihood had vanished, and what the assembly directly associated with it was that he sat in meditation in the main hall every night. If anyone had tampered with it, he should have been the first to know; since he showed no reaction, who then was most likely to be the thief? In everyone’s mind it went without saying! From then on, though no one in the temple, high or low, said it openly, whenever they saw Master Guangqin, not one of them did not turn white eyes on him. The ancients said: ‘Pointed at by ten thousand men, one dies without sickness.’ Under the silent rejection of the crowd, he did not utter a single word of explanation, nor did he give rise to the least thought of discontent or resentment. Thus more than a week passed; the others still glared at him in anger, yet he remained as if bathed in the spring breeze. Only then did the supervising monk and the incense-lamp monk come forward and reveal the answer to this case. It turned out that the incense money had not been lost at all; the two masters, the supervisor and the incense-lamp, had merely wished to use this matter to test what kind of practice Master Guangqin had trained in during his thirteen years on the mountain! They had not expected that even under the anger of the crowd he would be as if bathed in the spring breeze. After the supervisor and the incense-lamp monk made this clear, everyone felt ashamed. For more than a week they had daily turned their angry eyes on a man of perfect character, a practitioner who stood beyond things. Besides feeling a sense of guilt and unease, they each felt a deeper admiration and praise—yet Master Guangqin remained as he was, unmoved by praise or blame, gain or loss. (See The Cloud and Water Record of Elder Master Guangqin.)
[Why is this? Subhuti! As when I was formerly dismembered by King Kalinga, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life.]

The World-Honored One further clarified: why must one awaken to the fact that the paramita of patience is an illusion? As when I was formerly dismembered by King Kalinga, at that time I knew that all this was illusion (no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life), and so I patiently endured without anger.

The World-Honored One means: when I was formerly dismembered by King Kalinga, if I had clung to the paramita of patience—which is originally an illusion—as truly existent, then there would have been the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life, and because of the other’s unreasonableness and cruelty I would have been unable to endure, and would have given rise to a mind of hatred, unable to accomplish the paramita of patience.

There are two kinds of patience: one is forced endurance that takes the insult as real; the other is awakening to the fact that the insult is an illusion, watching the dream with wakened eyes, so that naturally it does not matter. The latter is the most lofty: with no person and no self, where does the insult come from? If the insult does not exist, why need one endure it? This endurance of non-endurance is great patience. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp

fascicle 27 records: “Dharma Master Sengzhao (one of the four philosophers under Master Kumarajiva) met with disaster at the hands of the ruler of Qin. As he was about to be executed, he spoke a verse: The four great elements are without a master; the five aggregates are originally empty. Facing the white blade with my head, it is like cutting the spring breeze (like the spring breeze blowing past; ‘cutting the spring breeze’ is an inversion, meaning the spring breeze cuts).” The Pagoda Inscription of the Great Ming Dynasty National Master Hanshan, the Five Teats Peak of Mount Lu, records: when Master Hanshan “was being tortured in the imperial prison, he suddenly entered chan samadhi. Though beaten with rods and burned with irons, it was as if it fell on wood and stone.” The Collected Works of Elder Zibai records: when Master Zibai “was interrogated and underwent all the torments of punishment in his decline, all his attendants’ hearts were about to drop, yet the Master was like idle clouds and still water, wholly without a thing.”

[King Kalinga] Formerly, when the Buddha was practicing in the causal stage, there was a King Kalinga, violent, evil and arrogant. At that time the Buddha was cultivating chan samadhi outside the city, and King Kalinga led his palace women out to tour and view. The maidens left the king and came to the Buddha’s place, and the Buddha spoke the Dharma for them. Seeing this, the king gave rise to an evil mind and asked the Buddha: Have you attained the fruit of arhatship? The Buddha said he had not. Have you attained the fruit of anagamin? The Buddha answered: No. The king said: Then do you, with a body that still has the affliction of desire, give free rein to looking at women? The Buddha said: Though I have not cut off the fetter of desire, in my mind there is truly no desire or clinging. The king then tested him: he cut off the Buddha’s ear, yet the Buddha’s countenance did not change. The ministers remonstrated with the king, wishing him to stop, but the king would not listen; he further cut off his nose (pronounced “yi”) and his hands, yet the Buddha’s marks remained perfect, without the slightest change. Then heaven rained sand and stones. The king’s heart was greatly terrified, and he went to the Buddha’s place to repent and beg for compassion. The Buddha said: My mind has no hatred and no desire. The king said: Great Virtue, how do you know your mind has no hatred? The Buddha said: If I have no hatred, may this body be restored as before. Having made this vow, his body was at once restored. The king repented all the more and thereupon entered the Buddha’s gate. [The fetter of desire] One of the five fetters. The affliction of desire binds people to birth and death within the three realms so that they cannot escape. The five fetters: the fetter of desire, the fetter of anger, the fetter of pride, the fetter of envy, the fetter of stinginess. “Fetter” is another name for affliction, because affliction can bind living beings and cause them to turn about within the three realms.

The World-Honored One uses his own experience to show that only by not clinging to marks can one truly be patient; only by not clinging to marks can one, amid circumstances, not give rise to habitual reactions. This also confirms that the absence of the four marks is the wondrous method for subduing the mind (see Chapter Three).
The Maha Prajna Paramita Sutra
fascicle 22

the Chapter on the Six Perfections Embracing One Another, the Sixty-Eighth, says: “The Buddha says: A bodhisattva dwelling in the virya paramita, from the first arising of the intention up to sitting at the place of enlightenment, if in the meantime human or non-human beings come to dismember him limb by limb, the bodhisattva thinks: ‘Who is it that cuts me? Who is it that severs me? Who is it that robs me?’ And he thinks again: ‘I have gained great benefit, for I took on this body for the sake of living beings, and living beings have come of themselves to take it.’ At that time the bodhisattva rightly recollects the true mark of all dharmas, and dedicates this merit, shared with living beings, to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, not toward the stage of shravakas or pratyekabuddhas. This is a bodhisattva dwelling in the virya paramita taking up the kshanti paramita.”
[Virya] In Chinese translation, “diligence,” one of the six perfections. [Kshanti] In Chinese translation, “patience,” one of the six perfections.

Master Hanshan says: “All living beings’ suffering of birth and death is accomplished through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, adorned with merit and wisdom, is reached through having no self. Because I is set against things, right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger grow; the self-nature grows turbid, and the mind-ground darkens; the mind-ground darkening, all evils grow; all evils growing, all sufferings gather; all sufferings gathering, birth and death are prolonged! All this is brought about by the self. How grave it is! The harm done by the self is like a strongly walled city with firm soldiers—how easily broken? ... Therefore, at every place where a thought stirs, test it with patience; at every place where a foot moves, put patience first; at every place of turning and composing the countenance, hold to patience; at every place of joy, anger, sorrow and happiness, verify it with patience. In this way the mind dares not stir rashly, the body dares not act rashly, affairs dare not be done rashly, and feelings dare not be expressed rashly. Hence Laozi said: Dare not, and so be first in the world. ‘Dare not’ is another name for patience. Because of daring not and so being first in the world, patience is the first practice for becoming a Buddha. In this way, when patience is great and I am small, patience can robe me and can also robe things; the virtue of benefiting self and others has nothing beyond this. Hence it is said: the robe of gentleness and patience—this is why.” (Dream Roam Collection
Showing the Chan Person Fajin)

Whether one has any certainty about ending birth and death can be tested from two ends: one is the end of favorable circumstances and success, the other is the end of adverse circumstances and affliction. Do you in both cases leave marks—not giving rise to mind or thought toward circumstances, not running after circumstances?

[Why is this? When I in former times was dismembered limb by limb, if I had had the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, I should have given rise to hatred.]

Why must there be no four marks? When I on that day was dismembered joint by joint by King Kalinga, if I had taken this dismemberment as real (had the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being, the mark of a life), I would have given rise to hatred.

Knowing illusion, one at once leaves it; leaving illusion, one is at once awakened. Since there is no self, where is the insult? With no self, who is there to receive the insult? This is the method of taking away the firewood from under the cauldron.

That the World-Honored One had no four marks when he was dismembered joint by joint in former times is because he had truly realized that “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false” and that “knowing all dharmas to be without self, one accomplishes patience.” How is this truly realized? Master Hanshan gave a most penetrating teaching in the essay in the Dream Roam Collection

Showing the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang—examining the mind amid circumstances in the midst of the dharma of birth and death, intimately seeing through, until one reaches the place of no doubt and then stops. It is copied out below:
The Buddhas and Patriarchs teach people to realize the patience of non-arising of dharmas at once within birth and death
(“patience of the non-arising of dharmas,” shortened to patience of non-arising; true wisdom resting securely on the principle of true suchness, which is neither born nor extinguished)

, and they always wonder that one deludedly sees birth and death within the non-arising. These words are like telling a dream to a market dweller: the hearers are certainly not without being roused and emboldened
(the hearers cannot but be moved and inspired)

, yet they have not realized the truth. In short, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients valued true realization: they simply wished to intimately see through within the dharma of birth and death, and there is no other extraordinary place. I have seen children who fear ghosts: whenever they walk in the night and something suddenly seems to follow them, they are greatly terrified; though a kind mother skillfully explains that it does not exist, they still do not believe it, and only stop when they themselves believe without doubt. If one reaches the place of no doubt oneself, then even if a ghost were to frighten him, he will laugh and let it go.

In former days I traveled to the frontier, and with a sturdy soldier rode by night. Beside the road was a stone; the horse suddenly saw it and was greatly startled, nearly falling to the ground. Thereupon
(so)
I pulled up the reins and whipped it with all my strength, riding around the stone in circles several tens of times, and still led it to look closely
(and led the horse to see clearly that this was a stone and not a monster)

for a long while, only then did it gallop freely away; from then on the horse was not startled by anything it met. From this I knew that a person wandering the perilous road of birth and death, examining the mind amid circumstances, must be like this and no other
(whip the horse around the stone, make it look closely, until it is without doubt and without fear, and only then stop)
. Therefore the Avatamsaka uses Sudhana to represent realization
(so the Avatamsaka Sutra uses the youth Sudhana’s fifty-three visits to make clear how true realization is done)
, passing through a hundred cities and visiting many good teachers. As for the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, he likewise hesitated
(hesitated, wavered)
and waited to be urged before entering. And when he entered, he indeed attained the great gate of cool liberation
(truly realizing that the mountain of knives and mass of fire are illusions)
. Is this not what is meant by whipping the horse around the stone and making it look closely?
(Is this not precisely to make him “whip the horse around the stone and make it look closely” and intimately see through?)
From this we see that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have no other strength: it is simply that they can look closely at the world’s
(worldly)

marks. What people fear—is it not birth and death and calamity? Yet the Buddhas and Patriarchs wish to make people realize the patience of non-arising therein, and further plainly say that within the non-arising one deludedly sees birth and death
(the Buddhas, within manifest birth and death, see only non-arising; living beings, within serene non-arising, deludedly see birth and death)
. Alas! What does this really mean? If not
(if not)
looking closely until one reaches the place of no doubt, then in my view, though the Compassionate One skillfully explain it, one will
(probably)
still hardly avoid terror.
Recently I
(I recently)
, because I propagated the Dharma, met with disaster and provoked the sage’s wrath
(the Master, because he propagated the Dharma, was slandered; the emperor was enraged, and he was arrested, thrown into prison, tortured for a confession, his life or death uncertain)
, like white-day thunder, so that hearers stopped their ears. From the time I was arrested until I left
(was exiled from the capital)

, more than two hundred days, I underwent indescribable sufferings. From beginning to end, I looked at a single thought of joy in myself and found it had not diminished at all from former times, and all who saw it were amazed as at something extraordinary. Yet birth and death and calamity are what others would be startled by on my behalf; and when they saw that my joy was undiminished, they were startled again. I am not startled by what they are startled by, while they are startled by what I am not startled by—perhaps there is a Way in this!

Attendant Qi, not grudging a journey of three thousand li, came to face the calamity and questioned me in the dark prison. Afterwards, by the imperial grace, I was banished to Lingnan, and Qi accompanied me on the boat, so I wrote this as a farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is precisely what people fear; do they not hear of my joy as though it were a dream?
(At the juncture of birth and death, this is precisely what people dread; yet to hear that my joy is not diminished in the least—is it not like hearing someone tell of a dream?)
Another day, when I test you in the field of quiescent extinction, do not take today’s words as dream talk

(when another day you realize the patience of non-arising (in the field of quiescent extinction), you will yourself verify that what I say is true. [Field of quiescent extinction] The realm in which the patience of non-arising is realized—delusion exhausted and truth revealed, quiescent extinction appearing before one)
, do not take today’s words as dream talk
(Dream Roam Collection
Showing the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang)
[Subhuti! Again I recall the past: for five hundred lives I was the Patience Sage. In those lives I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life.]

The World-Honored One continued: Subhuti! Again I recall the past: for five hundred lives I was the Patience Sage. In those five hundred lives I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a living being, no mark of a life.

[The Patience Sage] Shakyamuni Buddha, in the causal stage, was the Patience Sage and cultivated the practice of patience. [In those lives] In those five hundred lives. “Those” means “those”; “the lives” refers to the “five hundred lives” of the preceding sentence. Tang dynasty
Yijing’s translation: “Again I recall the past: for five hundred lives I was the Patience Sage. At that time I had no such notions.”

Master Yongjia’s Song of Realizing the Way says: “My teacher (Shakyamuni Buddha) saw the Burning Lamp Buddha; for many kalpas he had been the Patience Sage.” That is to say, when the World-Honored One was practicing in the causal stage, the reason he could see the Burning Lamp Buddha and receive the prediction was that for many kalpas he had been the Patience Sage. From this we see that the one practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice for becoming a Buddha.

In studying the Diamond Sutra there is one common question: how can one leave the four marks? Where should one begin? The point of entry for leaving the four marks is the practice of the paramita of patience: whatever one does, one should endure it. At all times and in all places, endure it, test it, and keep it up. At first patience is small and the self is great; later patience is great and the self is small; advancing without slackening, keeping it up, one comes to have no mark of a self! Once the mark of a self is extinguished, the other three marks are gone as well. The four marks are illusion, and the paramita of patience is also illusion; using illusion to extinguish illusion, one is a step further from illusion.

Dharma Master Daozheng, in the book Elder Master Guangqin’s Practice Examination Questions, writes: “On the path of practice there are examination questions every day and every hour. In the field for selecting Buddhas, each person hands in his own report card.” “We may read the Diamond Sutra first thing in the morning—‘All marks whatsoever are delusive and false,’ ‘Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness’—that is how we read the text. But if someone angrily scolds us, and scolds us with accusations that are wholly unjust, we at once set the Diamond Sutra aside and treat this situation as real, and begin to feel hurt and wronged. We do not remember at all: ‘All marks whatsoever are delusive and false.’ We begin to spin around following delusive marks; not only do we grasp at marks, we also let our minds move, and not only do our minds move, we grieve greatly, and we are not at all ‘unmoving in suchness.’ So after reading the sutra for several decades, the moment an applied question is tested we die a miserable death. If someone says that our studying Buddhism is all a sham and that we do not truly study, we hear it and feel very unconvinced. But if an examination comes, we confess without being pressed, showing that we have in fact learned nothing of what the Buddha taught us. What paramita of patience—set it aside for now, let us first argue a bit and cry a bit before anything else.”
[Therefore, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should leave all marks and give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]
For this reason, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should leave all marks and give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Above it was said that the first paramita is illusion and the paramita of patience is illusion, meaning that one should cultivate while leaving marks. Now it is said further that even when first giving rise to the mind one should give rise to it while leaving marks. Thus we know that “leaving all marks” runs through the entire bodhi path from beginning to end.

[Therefore] A phrase that carries on from what precedes and leads into what follows. [Leaving all marks] Leaving the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life, as well as the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. [Giving rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] Giving rise to the great mind of becoming a Buddha and saving living beings.

[One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells, then it does not dwell.]

One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind without love and hate, taking and rejecting. If the mind has any dwelling or clinging, that dwelling and clinging is wrong.

[If the mind dwells, then it does not dwell] If the mind has dwelling and clinging, this dwelling and clinging is not (that is, it does not dwell). Why is this? Because if the mind dwells, it is turned about by circumstances, and this is delusion. “If the mind dwells, then it does not dwell” returns once more to what Subhuti asked at the beginning of this sutra: “How should one abide?” Therefore the answer to how one should abide is: do not abide in marks.
